title: My grandfather's bicycle

paragraphs.text: The first ride was not quite the triumphant moment I had imagined. The saddle was too high, the brakes squeaked, and halfway down my grandmother's street the chain came off, to the great amusement of her neighbours. Tomás, when I told him, simply laughed and said that every bicycle needs time to get used to its rider.

'It's a good bike,' he said eventually. 'They don't make them like this any more. But if you want it to look like this again,' he added, pointing to an old catalogue on the wall, 'you're going to have to do most of the work yourself.' He then offered me a corner of his workshop on Saturday mornings.

These lessons, he insisted, had to be written down in a notebook, and every week he checked mine carefully to make sure I had copied his diagrams correctly. Anything I had got wrong had to be copied out again before I was allowed to pick up a tool.

In the end, the answer came from one of my grandfather's photographs. In it, he is standing proudly beside the bicycle on the day he bought it, and although the picture is in black and white, he had written the name of the colour on the back in pencil. Tomás knew a supplier who still made it.

For months it stayed exactly where it was. Every time I visited my grandmother, I would glance at it, feel a pang of guilt and look away. It was only when she mentioned, quite casually, that she was thinking of giving it to the scrapyard that I finally made up my mind to do something about it.

The person who enjoys it most, though, is my grandmother. When I rode it to her house for the first time, she stood at the window for a long while without saying anything. Then she went to fetch the box of photographs, and we spent the rest of the afternoon looking through them together.

This method drove me mad at first. I wanted instructions, diagrams, a clear list of steps. Only gradually did I realise that he was teaching me to look properly, to listen to the sound a chain makes when it needs oil and to feel when a bolt has been tightened enough.

items.hint: The writer 'tried hard to ignore' the bicycle. What happened to it next?
items.explanation: E ('For months it stayed exactly where it was') follows on from trying to ignore the bicycle, and ends with the decision to do something, which leads to the first step in the next paragraph.

items.hint: Tomás studied the frame 'before delivering his verdict'. What was the verdict?
items.explanation: B begins with the verdict ('It's a good bike,' he said eventually) and the offer of a corner of the workshop, which leads to 'So began the strangest apprenticeship'.

items.hint: Tomás 'rarely explained anything'. How did the writer feel about this way of teaching?
items.explanation: 'This method' in G refers to Tomás watching and then showing, never explaining. C cannot fit: it describes notebooks and diagrams, which contradicts 'He rarely explained anything'.

items.hint: No paint sample matched the original colour. How was the problem solved?
items.explanation: 'In the end, the answer came from one of my grandfather's photographs' solves the paint problem, and links back to the box of photographs in the first paragraph.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'Those early problems'. Which paragraph describes problems?
items.explanation: A describes the first ride and its problems (high saddle, squeaky brakes, the chain coming off), which the next paragraph calls 'Those early problems'.

items.hint: After people in the street, who enjoys the bicycle 'most, though'?
items.explanation: F contrasts the strangers who ask about the bicycle with the person who enjoys it most, the grandmother. C is the extra paragraph.

title: First week in Lisbon

paragraphs.text: My first lecture, when it finally came, was humbling. I had assumed that my Portuguese would be good enough to follow the classes, but the professor spoke at tremendous speed, with an accent quite unlike the one in my textbook, and made jokes that the whole room understood except me. I filled two pages with notes and could make sense of almost none of them.

Walking home afterwards through the empty streets, I thought back to the evening I had arrived, sitting on my suitcase and wondering whether to leave. It seemed much longer ago than six days. Lisbon had not changed in that time, but something in me clearly had.

The flat, when I finally found it at the top of a steep, cobbled street, looked nothing like the photographs. The kitchen was tiny, the window in my bedroom would not close properly, and there was no sign of the washing machine the advert had promised. I sat on my suitcase and seriously considered booking a flight home.

Her brother, who had studied in London, was even more helpful. He lent me his old textbooks, showed me the cheapest place to eat near the faculty and drove me to the university on my very first morning so that I would not get lost on the way.

That evening also marked the beginning of an arrangement that would last the whole year. In return for her help with my Portuguese, I helped Inês prepare for an English exam she was dreading. We met twice a week at the café downstairs, and the owner soon started bringing our coffees without being asked.

The next morning, however, I discovered that friendliness has its limits. At the university's international office, a queue of exchange students stretched along the corridor and out into the courtyard. After three hours, I reached the front, only to be told that one of my documents needed an official stamp from my home university.

The real test came on Friday night, when Inês took me to a birthday party where nobody else spoke English. For the first hour I hardly said a word. Then someone asked me about football, a subject on which I have strong opinions in any language, and before I knew it I was arguing passionately, and very ungrammatically, about the best team in Spain.

items.hint: The writer had only seen the flat 'in photographs'. What was it really like?
items.explanation: C describes the flat, which 'looked nothing like the photographs', and the writer considering going home. The next paragraph explains 'What stopped me'.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'the problem'. Which paragraph introduces a problem?
items.explanation: F contrasts the friendliness of the neighbours with the queue at the international office and the missing stamp, which is 'the problem' that took four days to sort out.

items.hint: Inês says 'Nobody understands that professor'. Which paragraph is about a professor?
items.explanation: A describes the first lecture and the professor nobody could follow, which Inês then comments on.

items.hint: Inês helped the writer 'that evening'. What did that evening lead to?
items.explanation: 'That evening also marked the beginning of an arrangement' picks up 'that evening' and introduces their language exchange.

items.hint: The next paragraph refers to 'that night'. Which paragraph describes a night out?
items.explanation: G describes the Friday night party where the writer argued 'very ungrammatically', which leads to 'I made dozens of mistakes that night'.

items.hint: Who walked home 'afterwards', and what did they remember?
items.explanation: B ('Walking home afterwards') follows the party and looks back to the writer sitting on the suitcase, which the final paragraph mentions again. D is the extra paragraph: no brother is ever mentioned.

title: The club that refused to die
topic: a village saves its football club

paragraphs.text: Since then, the changes have been remarkable. Attendances have more than doubled, the café is busy every morning, and the youth teams have produced three players who have gone on to professional clubs. On the pitch, the first team has won promotion twice in five years.

The housing developers, however, refused to give up. They offered the owner twice the amount the village had raised, hired lawyers to challenge the campaign, and for a few tense days it looked as if all the effort had been wasted.

Not everyone was enthusiastic. Some residents argued that the money would be better spent on the village school or the bus service, and a few wrote angry letters to the local paper accusing the campaign of putting football before more important things. These criticisms stung, but the organisers took them seriously.

Margaret Holt, now in her eighties, has little patience with such worries. 'Of course it's slow,' she told me when I visited. 'That's democracy. But nobody can ever sell this club from under us again, and that's worth a few long evenings in the village hall.'

All that changed one wet morning in February, when the club's owner announced that he could no longer afford to keep it going. The debts, he explained, had grown beyond anything he could manage, and unless a buyer could be found within six weeks, the club would be closed down and the ground sold for housing.

With two days to go before the deadline, the total stood at just over ninety per cent of what was needed. It seemed that the effort would fall agonisingly short. Then, late on the final evening, a single anonymous donation arrived that covered the rest.

It was at that meeting that a retired teacher named Margaret Holt made a suggestion that most people initially dismissed as absurd. If no buyer could be found, she said, why should the village not buy the club itself? Each household could contribute what it could afford, and the club would belong to everyone.

items.hint: The next paragraph begins 'The announcement caused uproar'. Which announcement?
items.explanation: E contrasts the club's quiet history ('All that changed') with the owner's announcement, which the next paragraph refers to.

items.hint: The previous paragraph describes a crowded meeting in the village hall.
items.explanation: 'It was at that meeting' refers back to the meeting in the village hall, and Margaret Holt's suggestion is 'the idea' that 'spread faster than anyone could have predicted'.

items.hint: The next paragraph begins 'In response' and mentions 'doubters'.
items.explanation: C describes the critics who thought the money should go elsewhere; the campaign's promise is the response, and it 'won over many of the doubters'.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'who sent the money'. Which paragraph describes a mysterious payment?
items.explanation: F describes the anonymous donation that arrived on the final evening, so 'Nobody has ever discovered who sent the money' follows naturally.

items.hint: The previous paragraph ends with the first annual meeting. What has happened 'since then'?
items.explanation: A ('Since then') describes the club's success, and the next paragraph begins 'Success has brought its own challenges'.

items.hint: Some members worry about long, heated meetings. Who has 'little patience with such worries'?
items.explanation: D responds to the worries about slow decisions and long meetings. B is the extra paragraph: it describes the developers fighting back, which does not fit the sequence of events anywhere.

title: Five minutes at the microphone
topic: trying stand-up comedy for the first time

paragraphs.text: I did not, mainly because my sister was standing in front of it. When my name was called, I walked to the microphone with my notes in my pocket and my heart beating so loudly that I was sure the audience could hear it. For the first thirty seconds, nobody laughed at all.

Then I tried the routine on a real audience: my family, gathered for Sunday lunch. My father laughed in all the right places. My mother asked whether I was really going to tell strangers about the salsa. My sister said nothing at all, which worried me more than anything else.

My sister, it turned out, had secretly booked herself a slot as well, and her routine about our family was considerably funnier than mine. The audience clearly preferred her, and so, I suspect, did the barman, who gave her a free drink.

What finally pushed me into it was my thirtieth birthday. My sister, tired of hearing me talk about it, gave me a present that consisted of a single piece of paper: a booking for a five-minute slot at an open-mic night in a pub near the station, exactly six weeks later.

When it was over, a man at the bar bought me a drink and told me I should come back the following month. I have no idea whether he meant it, but I chose to believe him. My sister, finally breaking her silence, said it was the best present she had ever given anyone.

Looking back, the most valuable lesson had nothing to do with comedy. I had spent years afraid of looking foolish, and that first night taught me that looking foolish is rarely as bad as we imagine. Sometimes, in fact, it is exactly what makes people warm to you.

In desperation, I signed up for a weekend workshop run by a comedian who had been performing for twenty years. Her advice was brutally simple. Stop trying to be clever, she told us, and talk about the things that embarrass you. The audience will forgive almost anything except a performer who is pretending.

items.hint: The writer always said they would try comedy 'one day'. What finally made it happen?
items.explanation: D explains 'What finally pushed me into it': the birthday present with a booked slot, which explains why the writer now needed material.

items.hint: The writer crossed out almost all their ideas. What did they do next, and why did they then write about embarrassing things?
items.explanation: 'In desperation' follows the failed notebook, and the advice to 'talk about the things that embarrass you' explains why the writer then wrote about the driving test and salsa.

items.hint: After practising alone in front of a mirror, who was the first real audience?
items.explanation: B ('Then I tried the routine on a real audience') follows the mirror practice, and the family's reactions explain why half the routine was rewritten before the show.

items.hint: The writer 'considered slipping out of the back door'. Did they?
items.explanation: 'I did not, mainly because my sister was standing in front of it' answers the previous sentence directly, and the silent first thirty seconds lead to 'Then something unexpected happened'.

items.hint: The next paragraph says 'I did go back the following month'. Who suggested coming back?
items.explanation: In E, a man at the bar tells the writer to 'come back the following month', which the next paragraph confirms. The sister also 'finally' breaks the silence that began in B.

items.hint: Before the final paragraph, the writer reflects on the most important lesson.
items.explanation: F reflects on the lesson about looking foolish, leading to the conclusion about being 'slightly braver'. C is the extra paragraph: the sister never performs in the story.
